text: Vitruvius recommends a city reservoir feeding a distribution tank with three compartments: one for public basins and fountains, one for baths, and one for private houses. In his Augustan Roman design, separating supplies protects public water from private diversion (Book VIII.6).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Verified primary context: Book VIII.6.1-2; chapter also specified in the stimulus.

text: In his Roman aqueduct recommendations, Vitruvius specifies a sloping masonry channel covered by a vault to shield the water from direct sun. The conduit is a protected route with a measured descent, rather than simply an open trench (Book VIII.6).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Verified primary context: Book VIII.6.1; chapter also specified in the stimulus.

text: Where hills interrupt an aqueduct route, Vitruvius recommends tunnelling at the required gradient. In loose earth or sand he calls for vaulted masonry and access shafts spaced along the route; his first-century BCE account treats ground conditions as a design constraint (Book VIII.6).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Verified primary context: Book VIII.6.3; chapter also specified in the stimulus.

text: Vitruvius argues that baked-clay water pipes are preferable to lead pipes, citing both taste and harm associated with lead. This is a recommendation in an Augustan Roman technical text, rather than evidence that every Roman water system avoided lead (Book VIII.6).
